subject: botany
question_text: Write a brief account on the class Dicotyledonae of Bentham and Hooker's classification.

verification.note: Chapter 8 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book pp.21-22), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star rank and NO year citation — so `stars` is 0 and `appearances` is empty by construction, not by omission. Only ONE botany source book is held: there is no TSBIE Basic Learning Material for botany (the copy in hand is physics-only) and no botany board paper in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the back-test against a real paper are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this chapter. This card is NOT-CHECKED — do not read that as checked-and-clean. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. BOOK ERRORS: the book spells the author "Bantham" (correct: Bentham), writes the series as "Bicarpellate" with "4 colorts" (correct: Bicarpellatae, 4 cohorts), and says the three classes are of "flowering plants" — but Gymnospermae is one of the three, and gymnosperms are seed plants, not flowering plants. Written here as seed plants (Phanerogams).

steps.label: The three classes
lines: In their book Genera Plantarum, Bentham and
Hooker divided the seed plants into three
Dicotyledonae is the largest of the three.
steps.why: The class asked about only makes sense inside the whole scheme, so the three classes come first.
common_mistakes: Writing that they divided the FLOWERING plants into three classes. Gymnosperms are seed plants but not flowering plants.
Putting Gymnospermae last. Bentham and Hooker placed it between the two.
steps.memory_tip: Three classes in their order: Dicots, Gymnosperms, Monocots. The gymnosperms sit in the middle.
steps.margin_note: Name all three classes even though the question asks only about one.

steps.label: Sub-classes and Polypetalae
steps.why: The three sub-classes are named from the corolla, so the name itself shows which one a plant belongs to.
common_mistakes: Writing Monocotyledonae as a sub-class of Dicotyledonae. It is a separate class.
Mixing up the cohort counts. Polypetalae runs 6, 4, 5.
steps.memory_tip: Poly-petalae = free petals. Gamo-petalae = fused petals. Mono-chlamydae = one covering, so no separate calyx and corolla.
steps.margin_note: Name the three sub-classes, then the three series of Polypetalae with their cohort counts.

steps.label: Gamopetalae and Monochlamydae
lines: Monochlamydae has 8 series and no cohorts at
steps.why: The series are the next rank down, and the pattern is easy to hold: two sub-classes have three series each, the third has eight.
common_mistakes: Writing that Monochlamydae has cohorts. It has none.
Spelling it Bicarpellate. The series is Bicarpellatae.
steps.memory_tip: Three series, three series, eight series. Only Monochlamydae has no cohorts.
steps.margin_note: Give the series names with their cohort counts in brackets.

steps.label: Total families
lines: In this system a cohort means an order, and a
Genera Plantarum holds 202 families in all: 165
steps.why: The number is the fact examiners tick, and knowing that "natural order" means "family" stops the number from being meaningless.
common_mistakes: Giving the number for the whole book instead of for Dicotyledonae alone.
steps.memory_tip: 165 + 3 + 34 = 202. The dicots are the great majority.
steps.margin_note: The number 165 is the mark. The 202 total is a safe extra line.

insider_note: This question is a list of names and numbers. Set it out as a branching list, not as prose; an examiner ticks names, and names are hard to find inside a paragraph.
